note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FOLLOW THE CROWN
tiles.details: The archived plant views (panels 1 and 4) support the coarse fountain-form bunch and attached flowering habit. Kew describes erect robust culms mostly 80–100 cm (extremes 50–150 cm). A photographed bunch alone does not prove a measured ligule, species ID, or local voucher. Check true basal continuity before calling a clump rhizomatous.
tiles.short: Large, tightly tufted perennial; follow a shoot to its flowering panicle.
tiles.status: VISIBLE GROSS FORM — ROOTED LOCAL VOUCHER STILL NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
tiles.details: Kew GrassBase describes an eciliate membrane 8–15 mm; Gibson's Williamson County account reports a membranous portion 10–39 mm plus sheath-margin lobes to 5 mm. Measure the actual free membrane on an attached leaf with a 1-mm scale; source ranges differ, so neither is a universal cutoff. Existing gallery images do not expose a ruler-calibrated true ligule. Do not arrow a sheath lobe as the ligule.
tiles.short: Unfold the blade/sheath junction; find a conspicuous papery MEMBRANOUS ligule.

tiles.heading: 03 · TRACE THE ENTIRE PANICLE
tiles.details: Kew reports panicles approximately 20–40 cm long and 1–1.5 cm wide, while Williamson County specimens have aging open arrays about 30–62.5 cm long and 4–7.5 cm wide. Panel 2 shows a source-labelled dense head, but no verified ruler or complete age series. Do not use a single panicle-width threshold or color to identify the species.
tiles.short: Long, usually contracted panicle; aging branches may become more open.
tiles.status: REAL FLOWERING PHOTO — DIMENSIONS FROM LITERATURE

tiles.heading: 04 · MEASURE A MATURE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Collect only where permitted. At 10–20× photograph several ripe spikelets beside a 1-mm scale. The two persistent membranous glumes are roughly subequal, one-veined (Kew 2–3.5 mm each; Gibson about 2–2.7+ mm). Identify each glume separately before any fine anatomical arrow. The existing wide flowering photo does not resolve their veins.
tiles.short: One fertile floret; spikelet about 2–3.5 mm in Kew, 2.5–3.5 mm in Williamson County.

tiles.heading: 05 · FIND THE LEMMA AND ACTUAL AWN
tiles.details: Kew gives a 2–3.5-mm lemma and 0–4-mm awn; Gibson describes a roughly 2-mm lemma and awns commonly 0.1–1.5 mm, sometimes absent or to 4 mm. Dissect the lemma from both glumes and expose its tip, the palea and any true awn origin. A dark filament or bristle in a whole-head photo is not proof of an awn attachment.
tiles.short: Three-veined fertile lemma; awn absent or short, up to about 4 mm.

tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES + RELEASE GATE
tiles.details: Panel 3 is M. reverchonii, a DIFFERENT-species comparison: usually smaller fine leaves and a more airy head. Nimblewill (M. schreberi) sprawls and may root at lower nodes; nursery M. capillaris has pink plumes but is not a substitute for a wild locally verified plant. M. ×involuta stays on scientific hold; intermediate appearance is not proof of hybrid identity. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: locally verified attached rooted crown, complete panicle, 1-mm ligule and dissected glume/lemma/awn series plus matched seep muhly. NEEDS_SITE_QA: confirm three local JPEGs and one external image record, per-image CC BY/CC0 credits and rights, four existing comparison panels and arrow endpoints, and public mobile rendering. Retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
tiles.short: Separate smaller seep muhly by growth form AND measured collar/reproductive traits.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: LOOK HERE FIRST: find the large, coarse, tightly packed perennial CROWN, then follow the tall stalks to long narrow, often densely packed PANICLES. Photograph a complete head and a fresh blade. At the blade–sheath junction, unfold the blade to expose its relatively LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule; measure rather than guessing from bunch size or plumage color. Compare a mature single-flowered spikelet and awn with seep muhly; neither species is photo-proven solely by habit.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: WHOLE PLANT: take one level photo of the large upright basal bunch and top of the flowering stalk with ruler/frame-scale; today's first image is habit evidence only.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Kew GrassBase describes an eciliate membrane 8–15 mm; Gibson's Williamson County account reports a membranous portion 10–39 mm plus sheath-margin lobes to 5 mm. Measure the actual free membrane on an attached leaf with a 1-mm scale; source ranges differ, so neither is a universal cutoff. Existing gallery images do not expose a ruler-calibrated true ligule. Do not arrow a sheath lobe as the ligule.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Kew reports panicles approximately 20–40 cm long and 1–1.5 cm wide, while Williamson County specimens have aging open arrays about 30–62.5 cm long and 4–7.5 cm wide. Panel 2 shows a source-labelled dense head, but no verified ruler or complete age series. Do not use a single panicle-width threshold or color to identify the species.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Compared with M. reverchonii, Lindheimer usually has a much coarser, larger fountainlike crown, larger/stiffer blades, long relatively contracted panicles, and a longer membranous ligule. Kew/GrassBase describes Lindheimer ligules commonly 8–15 mm and seep ligules 2–4(–9) mm, but overlapping treatments mean the actual mature blade/sheath and mature spikelet must agree. The live hybrid M. ×involuta can be intermediate and must NOT be named from intermediate size alone. Nursery M. capillaris (including cultivars) is a separate nonlocal ornamental look-alike, not an acceptable substitute for wild local species photos.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

intro: LOOK HERE FIRST: find the large, coarse, tightly packed perennial CROWN, then follow the tall stalks to long narrow, often densely packed PANICLES. Photograph a complete head and a fresh blade. At the blade–sheath junction, unfold the blade to expose its relatively LONG papery MEMBRANOUS ligule; measure rather than guessing from bunch size or plumage color. Compare a mature single-flowered spikelet and awn with seep muhly; neither species is photo-proven solely by habit.
memory_rule: LINDHEIMER: BIG stiff fountain + relatively DENSE narrow head. Confirm LONG papery ligule with a mm scale; not color or height alone.
safety_note: Published GrassBase ligule ranges (Lindheimer often 8–15 mm; seep 2–4(–9) mm) overlap at some limits. Use multiple characters and a measured mature leaf; all existing arrows identify gross visible growth or seedhead structures only. The seep comparison photo is a DIFFERENT species. The hybrid M. ×involuta must not be inferred from plant size.
field_rule: First check SCALE and the BASAL BUNCH: Lindheimer muhly forms a large coarse, densely tufted fountain often around 0.8–1.5 m tall, with tall relatively contracted, densely flowered panicles. At the leaf collar a LONG MEMBRANOUS ligule is the high-value confirmation; photograph it with a ruler rather than inferring it from plant size.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
